blocks.text: Jerusalem was both a royal center and a center of worship in the southern Levant, bringing kingship, temple worship, and imperial pressure together in one place. Its history as the Davidic capital and temple center, and later as a focal point of exile, return, pilgrimage, judgment, and hope for restored worship, gives weight to the vision in verses 2–4. The nations are drawn not merely to a prominent city but to the place from which Jehovah's instruction and judgment are pictured as reaching many peoples.

One debated way of reading Isaiah's wider treatment of the nations highlights a deliberate tension: Judah, Israel, foreign nations, and even powerful empires are subject to judgment, yet the nations can also be portrayed as learning, worshiping, and sharing in restoration. Isaiah 2:2–4 presents that hopeful side especially clearly. Many peoples seek divine instruction, accept Jehovah's decisions between nations, and turn weapons into agricultural tools.

Micah 4:1–3 contains close verbal material also found in Isaiah 2:2–4: Zion is elevated, divine instruction goes out, disputes among peoples are settled, and weapons are transformed for agriculture. The precise literary relationship between the passages is debated, but the parallel makes clear that this vision circulated in closely related prophetic form rather than appearing only in Isaiah's wording.

The Great Isaiah Scroll preserves an almost complete witness to all sixty-six chapters of Isaiah. It is broadly aligned with the Masoretic textual tradition while containing thousands of differences, ranging from spelling to substantive readings. Other Isaiah manuscripts and interpretive writings from Qumran also show that the book was actively copied and interpreted. The classification and significance of these differences remain matters of scholarly discussion.
